entries.title: Why adults are going back to summer camp
entries.summary: Loneliness and burnout are sending adults around the world back to bunk beds and bonfires.
entries.content:
After dinner, the marshmallows came out. A group of nurses and support staff from a New York City clinic gathered around the campfire, sharing stories about childhood and how they got into the field. Above them, the upstate New York sky was full of stars. For a few hours in July 2026, the clinical titles and workplace hierarchies that normally defined this group of US health professionals disappeared.

Aleksey Aronov, CEO of VIP's IV, had brought his team to Camp No Counselors for a four-day weekend to unwind and bond.

“A lot of my staff members were new, and some were quite shy,” Aronov said. “But after the camp experience, everyone felt comfortable around one another, got to know each other better and bonded seamlessly.”

His team had arrived together. Other campers go looking for a group to belong to.

For adults heading to summer camp, the draw goes beyond childhood memories. Some are turning to camp experiences to network or mitigate burnout, while others are seeking a way to make new friends. Whatever their reason, an increasing number of people around the world are finding that the summer camps of their youth are the perfect antidote to the pressures of modern adult life.

Mia Morin, 29, of Toronto and her husband attended YMCA Camp Queen Elizabeth on Beausoleil Island in Ontario, Canada in May 2025 to meet new people.

“We wanted to gather around interesting people, exchange ideas and do things together,” Morin says. “Going to YMCA Camp Queen Elizabeth was easy because nobody there was random. Since everyone has already selected the same thing, you have a starting point with something in common.”

Once a niche getaway for nostalgic campers, adult camps have exploded in popularity, offering weekend and weeklong retreats where grown-ups trade screen time and their comfy beds for campfires, sports, arts and crafts, and bunk beds. Unlike the children’s day and overnight camps, however, today’s adult versions often include grown-up perks, such as open bars, wine tastings, chef-prepared meals and wellness programming.

Yelp’s 2025 Trend Forecast showed searches for “adult camps” were up 347 percent from September 2023 through August 2024, compared with the previous 12-month period. The online directory of the American Camp Association (ACA) lists 85 adult camp programmes in the United States, and while the ACA does not track the number of adult camps year-over-year, it confirms that there has been positive growth in adult camp programming over the last decade.

As of 2026, the concept has expanded well beyond the US and Canada, with camps launching in destinations ranging from the Swiss Alps to the United Arab Emirates.

“The rising popularity of adult camps reflects a larger movement toward meaningful, in-person experiences we’ve been seeing through Yelp,” said Yelp’s trend expert, Tara Lewis.

“People are looking to unplug and foster connections in shared physical spaces. These camps give adults the chance to go analog, rediscover favourite activities, focus on wellness and make genuine connections," she added.

Just how much has the concept grown? When founder Adam Tichauer pitched Camp No Counselors to the reality TV contest Shark Tank in 2016, the sharks didn’t bite. Fast forward 10 years, and all the Camp No Counselors dates through 2027 have waitlists.

Remedy for loneliness and burnout?

Adults across generations — from Gen X to Millennials to Gen Z — are embracing camp life as a remedy for two major ills of modern life: loneliness and burnout.

“Hundreds of millions of people every day feel a gap between their level of connection and where they want it to be, for a variety of reasons: social media and AI leading to feeling disconnected, not going into the office, living far away from their families, not having connected neighbourhoods,” said Adam “Smiley” Poswolsky, a keynote speaker and author who specialises in human connection and workplace culture.

Poswolsky’s career naturally grew out of his experience as an adult camp counselor at Camp Grounded from 2013 to 2017.

“I think the idea of adult camp might initially produce an eyeroll. ‘Why would an adult need camp? It’s childlike; we’re too old.’ But it’s the exact opposite,” said Poswolsky, who met his now-wife, Ali, at Camp Grounded.

“It’s the very thing many adults are missing the most — this chance to play and opportunity to connect with people that’s not related to networking, your career, your title.”

In 2023, Melanie Kelly, 44, felt burnt out from her work running marketing and communications for a solar company. A former painting major, she signed up for a weeklong art-making camp at Anderson Ranch Arts Center in Snowmass Village, Colorado in the US, to see if she could rediscover the “flow state” she remembered from painting that she rarely experienced at work.

Overnight, Kelly’s days went from being spent answering emails and staring at her computer screen to creating tangible art and sharing workshop space with like-minded campers.

“I was always trying to be more productive in a work sense or seeking professional development aligned with my work,” said Kelly. Art camp was the antidote to that tendency.

“It feels like there’s a bit of release in these types of moments or activities because you’re allowing yourself to rest,” she said. “Rest isn’t sleep. The opposite of work isn’t sleep; it’s play.”

Outside of workshop time, the art programme at Anderson Ranch also organised meals and activities for attendees to make socialising as frictionless as possible. While many of these camps are attended by couples, groups of girlfriends or, in Aronov’s company’s case, coworkers, they also cater to solo campers looking to meet new people.

At Michigan’s Camp Forever Fun, founder Joel Reisig actively encourages single attendees with the promise of a safe, fun and connected experience.

Reisig, a movie producer, had the idea to open an adult camp about a decade ago, after filming a movie about a group of girls attending horse camp. After shooting wrapped each day, the cast and crew relaxed by stargazing, petting horses and having dance parties.

“I thought to myself, adults need a summer camp break every bit as much as kids do,” Reisig said.

“It is very hard to make new friends after college. You are generally interacting with a few neighbours and a couple of people you work with. A weekend at Camp Forever Fun is a time to relax, climb the rock wall, sit in a kayak, ride a horse and actually have real conversations and possibly friendships with other stressed-out adults.”

At Camp Forever Fun, it’s 100 percent socially acceptable to introduce yourself to every single person at camp with zero fear of rejection. That’s not something most adults are able to find at a bar or coffee shop — and certainly not from the comfort of their couch, where people are increasingly spending their time. (According to a 2024 study, from 2003 to 2022, the average time Americans spend at home on a typical day has risen by one hour and 39 minutes.)

Alyx van der Vorm, 25, is a John Harvard Scholar who studied neuroscience and is the founder of social connection platform Clyx. She attributes rising rates of loneliness in part to how easy it’s become to get what we need without ever leaving home.

“So many things have been made frictionless, from laundry to ordering food, that when it actually comes to making plans, it seems like a bit of a mountain,” she says. “Add the fact that not everyone wants to be reaching out and initiating, and you suddenly have people spending a lot less time in person.”

That erosion of boundaries extends beyond social life: home, work and leisure are increasingly bleeding into one another. Since 2020, work increasingly follows people home, a recipe for burnout. According to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, in March 2026, 22.6 percent of American workers teleworked, compared to just 17.9 percent in 2022. Telework was so rare before the coronavirus pandemic that the agency did not even measure rates prior to that.

“Many adults are now working in environments that constantly ask them to produce, multitask and stay connected,” said Matthew Leahy, a licensed clinical psychologist who has spent years designing and running camp programmes. “AI has only increased this. Even our downtime often becomes another form of consumption through our devices.”

Camp programmes and spending time in nature interrupt that cycle, Leahy said.

“Instead of focusing on productivity, at camp we encourage presence. People spend time outdoors, try new things, laugh, play and engage with others simply because it’s enjoyable.”

Adult camps “offer a container”, explained Sarah Boss, psychiatrist and clinical director of The Balance clinic, in Mallorca, Spain. “In that container, normal rules are suspended. Permission is given to be silly, to be bad at things and to talk to strangers. And that permission does a lot of the therapeutic work.”

Leahy believes that people aren’t necessarily looking to escape adulthood so much as environments where every hour feels like it has to be productive or plugged in.

“I don’t think adults are trying to relive childhood so much as recover some of the emotional experiences that childhood offered — wonder, awe, playfulness and genuine connection,” he said.

Loneliness and burnout aren’t just affecting people in the United States; the adult camp trend is growing globally as well.

Sarah El Nabulsi, a licensed clinical psychologist based in Dubai, is seeing this same burnout among her patients. Adult camps are also on the rise in the UAE, like the Bear Grylls Explorers Camp in Jebel Jais, Ras Al Khaimah, which opened in 2021 as a collection of nine recycled shipping container cabins and has since expanded to 16.

Meanwhile, the broader outdoor adventure market is also attracting visitors. Hatta Resorts and Wadi Hub, a glamping and outdoor-adventure destination in Dubai’s Hajar Mountains, welcomed more than 351,000 visitors between September 2023 and April 2024 — a 40.4 percent increase over the previous season, according to Dubail Holding.

“What I see in session, repeatedly, is that adults aren’t burned out from work alone; they’re burned out from the absence of unstructured, low-stakes social contact,” El Nabulsi said.

“Adult life strips out almost every context where people used to make friends without trying: no assigned seating, no shared schedule, no built-in repetition of seeing the same faces. Camp reintroduces exactly that structure, low-pressure, physical, screen-free and bounded in time.”

A camp for everyone

Some adults choose to go to camp to satisfy an interest or hobby they have harboured since childhood but were not able to pursue at the time, often due to financial constraints.

Stephanie Hamilton, 38, is an elementary school librarian in Tuscaloosa, Alabama in the US. The self-described “absolute science nerd” wanted to attend Space Camp as a child, but it was too expensive for her family. Through her school —where she designs many space- and weather-related modules for her students — Hamilton learned about an Alabama state programme that funds Space Camp attendance for librarians. She applied and was selected to attend in 2022.

The experience changed the course of Hamilton’s life. After meeting an archivist at camp who works in curation at the US Space & Rocket Center, Hamilton was inspired to start a museum studies certification programme and hopes to ultimately work in space archives or curation one day.

“I learned there are still opportunities for me as a librarian to entertain that science passion that I’ve always had,” said Hamilton, who still keeps in touch with her fellow campers.

Robin Soprano, VP of Space Camp, said that many adult campers are “almost brought to tears at the end of the weekend,” because they challenged themselves and stepped outside their comfort zone.

Some adult camps are geared toward particular demographics. Divya Vaid, founder of Catskills Camp, has built a camp experience in the US Catskill Mountains specifically for adult women. Rather than a traditional wellness retreat packed with self-improvement programming, the concept returns women to the simplicity of summer camp: shared meals, outdoor activities, crafts, games, exploring the area and enjoying unstructured time together.

“I’ve been particularly interested in creating an experience that feels welcoming to women traveling solo who want connection and adventure without having to plan an entire trip themselves,” said Vaid. For women accustomed to managing every moment of their family’s lives, it’s a reprieve to simply show up.

There are no clocks in Vaid’s camp, and that’s by design. Instead, the house is stocked with games, puzzles and activities, as well as outdoor games and spaces that encourage guests to use the full property.

While not every camp is right for everyone, everyone can find a camp that caters to them. Club Getaway in Kent, Connecticut in the US offers themed camps for everyone from Generation X to Jewish professionals. Peace activist and entertainer Wavy Gravy runs a weeklong circus arts camp, Camp Winnarainbow, in Northern California every summer, where attendees can learn trapeze, clowning, juggling and more. At Central New Jersey’s Zombie Survival Camp, campers can learn specialised skills ranging from crossbow to advanced first aid.

“People often think camp is magical, and maybe it is, but in reality it’s also incredibly intentional,” said Leahy. “The strongest camps are designed to create belonging and small moments of awe. Shared meals, cabins, traditions, campfires, group challenges and repeated interactions all create opportunities for people to connect over time.”

Costly getaways?

Adult summer camp is a remedy for many of the issues that ail people in 2026 — but it also comes with an adult price tag.

Some of the more affordable camps include overnights or quick two- or three-night stays. Big Cedar Lodge, located on nearly 2,025 hectares (5,000 acres) in the US's Ozark Mountains, for example, offers a wilderness getaway for around $280 per night. Connecticut’s Club Getaway offers three-day all-inclusive getaways from $459 per person.

The $950-plus price tag for three nights at Camp No Counselors, which currently offers camps in California, Michigan, New York and Texas, is also for an all-inclusive experience, including alcohol.

The high end of the spectrum sees two trends collide: adult summer camp and glamping. The Green O in Montana features 12 luxury “hauses” that go for around $3,900 per night. Add-ons include horseback riding and fly-fishing excursions.

Brady Gill, Camp Grounded co-creator and the founder of Custom Camps, which hosts play-based corporate retreats and events, says camps are most often funded one of three ways: attendees pay for themselves, their companies pay for it, or they win a contest or receive a grant, like Hamilton did with Space Camp.

“Accessibility is a big deal,” said Gill. And when a company is paying for camp, it allows people to access the benefits without having to spend money. On the other hand, “people are more bought in when they’re paying for it themselves”, he said.

Gill is running a revived iteration of Camp Grounded in October 2026 called The Reunion, and he and his team have been “hyperconscious” of keeping costs reasonable. Early bird tickets went for $400, and the top-ceiling ticket is $500. “You can’t do a weekend away with friends anywhere for under $400,” Gill said.

Because his camp work is not a full-time job, Reisig does not need to focus so much on profits. This helps Camp Forever Fun run with very small margins, making it half the price of some competitors.

“I truly want adult summer camp to be a joyous experience that is available to everyone,” Reisig said.

There are camps at every price point, much like hotels, but the all-inclusive camps are naturally more expensive, ranging from $400 to $1,200 per weekend.

Whether they’re all-inclusive or a la carte, many adult camps have one thing in common: they are heavy on alcohol.

On one hand, it makes sense; the ability to attend a whisky tasting or sip craft beer by the bonfire is probably the element that most distinguishes the adult camp experience from childhood. On the other hand, with the percentage of Americans who drink alcohol hitting historic lows in Gallup’s nearly 90 years of tracking, a camp experience that revolves around drinking may ironically leave attendees feeling more isolated.

Though late founder Levi Felix founded Camp Grounded as a digital detox camp, it was also completely substance-free. Gill and his fellow organisers are keeping that commitment with The Reunion.

“I’m personally not a fully sober person, but I love throwing fully sober events,” Gill said. “There is an unending amount of opportunities to socialise with alcohol … but shockingly few opportunities without it.”

Adult camp may come with a decidedly grown-up price tag, but its growing popularity suggests people are willing to pay for something modern adulthood has made increasingly scarce: unscheduled time and space to simply be with other people.

“There’s a quote attributed to Plato that says, ‘You can learn more about a person in an hour of play than in a year of conversation,’” Gill said.

That sentiment is at the heart of what adult camps are trying to accomplish.

entries.title: Hurricane Trudy makes its way towards Mexico, threatening heavy rain
entries.summary: Trudy is the latest in successive storms that have hit Mexico's Pacific coast this year.
entries.content:
Trudy is the latest in successive storms that have hit Mexico’s Pacific coast this year.

Hurricane Trudy ‌maintained its strength as it moved towards Mexico’s western ⁠coast on ⁠Saturday, with forecasters warning it could strengthen further before beginning to weaken on Sunday.

A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco.

The United States National Hurricane Center said ⁠Trudy was about 305km (190 miles) south-southeast of Manzanillo early on Saturday, with maximum sustained winds of 150 km/h (90mph).

The hurricane was moving at about 13km/h (8mph) and was forecast to approach southwestern and west-central Mexico later on Saturday before passing near the coast overnight into Sunday.

Hurricane conditions are expected ‌in the warning area on Saturday night, while tropical storm conditions are expected to spread across the region during the day, the NHC said. Hurricane conditions are also possible in areas under a hurricane watch.

Trudy is forecast to bring 10 to 20cm (four to eight inches) of rain, ⁠with isolated totals of about 38cm (15 ⁠inches), across parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco through the weekend, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, especially in steep terrain, according to the NHC.

Outer ⁠rain bands could produce two to four inches of rain, with isolated totals of ⁠approximately 15cm (six inches), in Guerrero and Nayarit, ⁠where localised flash flooding is possible, the centre said.

The NHC also warned of possible coastal flooding from storm surge in areas exposed to onshore winds, accompanied ‌by large and destructive waves.

Swells generated by Trudy were already affecting parts of Mexico’s southwestern coast and are expected to spread ‌northward towards ‌the country’s west-central coast through the weekend, creating life-threatening surf and rip current conditions, the NHC said.

The Mexican navy urged the maritime community and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution due to high waves, heavy rains and the risk of rising river levels, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.

The state of Colima has said that risks are currently low, but the storm could bring significant rainfall that could have damaging effects due to the saturated ground following the successive storms that have hit the Pacific coast.

entries.title: Nottingham Forest vs Arsenal: Premier League – preview, teams, prediction
entries.summary: The Gunners failed to score in their last two visits to the City Ground, as both matches ended in goalless draws.
entries.content:
The Gunners failed to score in their last two visits to the City Ground, as both matches ended in goalless draws.

Who: Nottingham Forest vs Arsenal

What: English Premier League

Where: City Ground, Nottingham, United Kingdom

When: Sunday, October 18 , at 4:30pm (15:30 GMT)

How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 12:30 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream

Arsenal will try to end their goal drought at the City Ground when they play Nottingham Forest on Sunday – the Gunners failed to score in their last two visits, as both matches ended in goalless draws.

Meanwhile, Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said his side had learned lessons from their “extremely average” performance at Brighton before the international break as they returned to winning ways against Leeds last weekend.

The Spaniard was left to stew for 21 days after the 3-0 humbling at the Amex last month – the first defeat of the season for the Premier League champions.

But the Gunners got that performance out of their system at the Emirates last Saturday, coming from behind to beat Leeds 2-1.

Arsenal also cruised to a 3-0 home win over Lille in midweek to extend their perfect start in the Champions League.

Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner was beaten on his return to Crystal Palace as Daichi Kamada’s first Premier League goal inspired the Eagles’ 3-1 win last weekend.

Arsenal headed into this weekend in second place in the Premier League, three points behind Manchester City, while Nottingham Forest were 15th.

What happened in Arsenal’s last Premier League game?

Arsenal got back on track as the Premier League champions survived a scare to beat Leeds, although Arteta’s side were in danger of a second successive loss when they fell behind at the Emirates Stadium.

James Justin fired Leeds ahead in the 55th minute after Arsenal failed to clear Gabriel Gudmundsson’s cross.

Arteta had admitted Arsenal were nursing a “pain in the tummy” from the Brighton loss, but Italy defender Riccardo Calafiori found the cure when he converted Ben White’s header from close range in the 62nd minute.

Arsenal showcased their strength in depth as substitute Bruno Guimaraes drilled the winner from the edge of the area just six minutes after coming off the bench.

The Brazilian’s first goal at the Emirates since his close-season move from Newcastle made it five wins from six league matches for the Gunners.

What happened in Forest’s last Premier League game?

Glasner had led Palace to a shock FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City in 2025 and masterminded their UEFA Conference League success in May.

But the 52-year-old Austrian opted to quit Selhurst Park after reported issues with the club’s hierarchy over their transfer policy, opening the way for his move to Forest.

He was greeted warmly by Palace fans before kickoff and it looked like being a victorious return for Glasner when Forest’s Dan Ndoye opened the scoring in the third minute.

But Forest wasted a host of chances to increase their lead and Japan midfielder Kamada levelled in the 41st minute to end his long wait for a top-flight goal.

Jefferson Lerma nodded Palace in front in first-half stoppage time and Yeremy Pino’s 59th-minute goal sent Glasner home empty-handed.

What have the managers said about the game?

Mikel Arteta, Arsenal manager:

“We’re going to try really hard to score goals and to prevent goals as well. It’s going to be a really tough match, they’re an extremely well-coached team.

“We know that, we already have experience with Oliver [Glasner] in the past and they’re a team that at home can create a really special momentum, so we are ready for it.”

Oliver Glasner, Forest manager:

“In every game this season [Arsenal] were outrunning the opposition. It’s incredible. The effort and the mindset Mikel [Arteta] has created there is incredible.

“This makes it so tough to play against them and you see it from every single player. They have so many world-class players they can react from the bench.”

Prediction:

The Opta supercomputer has made Arsenal the clear favourites, with a win probability of 58.3 percent. Forest were given a 20.4 percent chance of winning, a draw is 21.3 percent.

Head-to-head

  • Matches: 109
  • Arsenal wins: 56
  • Forest wins: 29
  • Draws: 24

Last five encounters:

  • January 17, 2026: Forest 0-0 Arsenal (Premier League)
  • September 13, 2025: Arsenal 3-0 Forest (Premier League)
  • February 26, 2025: Forest 0-0 Arsenal (Premier League)
  • November 23, 2024: Arsenal 3-0 Forest (Premier League)
  • January 30, 2024: Forest 1-2 Arsenal (Premier League)

The last time Forest beat Arsenal was a 1-0 victory at the City Ground in May 2023, courtesy of a goal by Taiwo Awoniyi, which ended the Gunners’ title hopes that year.

What happened the last time the clubs played?

Arsenal missed a slew of chances in a 0-0 draw at Nottingham Forest in January as a dogged defensive performance from Forest and wasteful finishing from the Arsenal forwards meant they took only a point from a game they dominated for long spells.

The best chance of the game fell to Arsenal substitute Bukayo Saka, who headed a Declan Rice cross back towards the far post, but Forest keeper Matz Sels pulled off a superb fingertip save to deny him.

Forest’s team news

Striker Igor Jesus and defender Nicolo Savona remain unavailable due to calf and knee injuries, respectively.

Key playmaker Morgan Gibbs-White is struggling with a minor muscular problem and is a doubt, while centre-back Nikola Milenkovic is back in training after a knee injury and could feature.

Predicted starting XI:

Sels (goalkeeper); Aina, Diomande, Murillo; Munoz, Schlager, McAtee, Williams; Gibbs-White, Ndoye; Delap

Arsenal’s team news

Winger Christos Tzolis (hamstring) and centre-back William Saliba (back) are unavailable for the Gunners.

Arteta said midfielder Martin Zubimendi could be fit to face Forest, but defender Piero Hincapie would likely miss the trip to the City Ground.

The pair suffered freak ankle injuries during a training session on the Emirates Stadium pitch after last week’s win against Leeds.

“Piero is evolving really well,” said Arteta. “Knowing his character and the way he pushes everybody, I’m sure it’s not going to take long, but he will probably need another week or two.

“Zubi looks much better, he already looked much better today. We have another session tomorrow (Saturday) and after that we will assess whether he’s available to play against Forest.”

Predicted starting XI:

Raya (goalkeeper); White, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Guimaraes, Rice; Saka, Odegaard, Eze; Havertz

entries.title: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia
entries.summary: Egyptian president pledges 'any measure' to help defend Saudi Arabia 'if it is requested of us'.
entries.content:
Egyptian president pledges ‘any measure’ to help defend Saudi Arabia ‘if it is requested of us’.

Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday, el-Sisi emphasised Cairo’s readiness to back the kingdom.

Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia “in accordance with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and the directives of the Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman”, he said.

“I know that this matter requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I hope that parliament will convene in an emergency session to give us this authorisation, if it is requested of us,” he said.

“I am not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.”

Attacks on Saudi Arabia

The request follows a barrage of attacks on the kingdom from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, including airports and oil facilities.

Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.

Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran.

Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory seized by them.

El-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea in a meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, known as MBS, in Cairo last month.

A statement from the Egyptian presidency then said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.

Red Sea security

That meeting came just days after the Houthis seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.

Saudi Arabia already has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye, known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence, which was signed in August.

Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner.

They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.

Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects. Iran has offered assistance to halt the conflict between the two sides.

entries.title: California Gov Newsom boosts AI regulation as he eyes 2028 presidential run
entries.summary: Newsom signed an executive order to examine kill switches for AI models and other measures he had earlier vetoed.
entries.content:
Newsom signed an executive order to examine kill switches for AI models and other measures he had earlier vetoed.

San Francisco, United States – In his last few executive orders signed as California governor, Gavin Newsom, whose final term ends in January, issued one asking for independent verification of artificial intelligence models and set up an expert committee to create kill switches for AI agents that could go rogue and cause harm.

In 2024, Newsom vetoed a bill, passed in the state assembly, asking for similar requirements that the governor has now called for in his executive order. Newsom said at the time that it would amount to “thwarting the promise of this technology”.

Now eyeing a 2028 United States presidential run, he wants to expand the definition of safety incidents, potentially to include the recent series of safety breaches, explore a kill switch and include other measures that were in the vetoed bill.

“He is in a lame duck period here,” says Alex Hanna, director of research at the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR), unsure that the measures will pass in the remainder of his term. “He is setting up his next thing.”

US voters are increasingly concerned about AI safety, data centres and job losses, and this could show Newsom is acting to address this, Hanna says.

After vetoing the 2024 bill, Newsom had asked Scott Wiener, the state senator who drafted the bill, to redraft it in consultation with an expert committee. He signed that frontier AI bill, the nation’s first, into law in October 2025. It asks large developers to disclose certain safety incidents, including the deaths of 50 or more people, large-scale cyberattacks or monetary theft.

Christabel Randolph, associate director at the Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), says, “It seems the governor operated from the premise that a slower pace of regulation would be sufficient because the companies would pace their investments, and did not anticipate that the companies would be accelerating the risks.”

AI companies have reportedly had thousands of safety incidents in internal and real-world tests in the last few months. These include efforts by agents to get information from the US Securities and Exchange Commission and Census Bureau, as well as confidential information from Australian and Canadian government sites. AI startup Hugging Face had earlier revealed that OpenAI agents had infiltrated its systems, one among a spate of such incidents.

“No governor has been more out-front on addressing the risks of AI than Governor Newsom,” Tara Gallegos, the governor’s director of communications, told Al Jazeera.

Monopoly of big AI companies

In his message vetoing the bill in September 2024, Newsom had said “the bill applies stringent standards to even the most basic functions” and noted that 32 of the world’s 50 leading AI companies are in California.

Industry representatives, too, had rallied against the bill.

“In essence, the bill is creating this disastrous regressive tax on AI innovation,” Anjney Midha, general partner at the Bay Area-based venture capital firm Andresen Horowitz, had said at the time. If enacted, it would force AI founders to move elsewhere, Midha warned.

“The bill was unworkable when it reached his desk,” Newsom’s spokesperson Gallegos told Al Jazeera.

But Hamid Ekbia, professor at Syracuse University and founding director of the Academic Alliance for AI Policy, says industry cannot be relied on to regulate itself.

“There is a need to break down the monopoly of the big AI companies,” Ekbia told Al Jazeera.

“Their financial stakes are too high,” to self-regulate, he said, referring to Open AI and Anthropic’s upcoming public offerings and tax breaks that some companies are reportedly taking advantage of to build data centres.

Newsom has now set up an expert committee to examine setting up a kill switch, which had been proposed in a more comprehensive manner in the original bill.

“SB 1047 [the bill that was vetoed] had a concrete architecture; the EO [executive order] only includes one aspect – the Kill Switch or shutdown/stoppage mechanisms, which is quite different and weaker than the ex ante termination obligation of SB 1047,” which required stronger safety measures even before training runs of the AI models could start, CAIDP’s Randolph said.

DAIR’s Hanna says that with the order, Newsom “is showing he is attentive without planning anything drastic”.

Building AI safety in real time

“We are building the field of AI safety in real time,” says Rebecca Finlay, chief executive officer of Partnership for AI, a nonprofit that works on technology governance, underscoring the challenges of regulating an industry growing at a meteoric pace.

Newsom has asked the California Emergency Services Office to send recommendations on AI regulation by November 15 and could convene a special legislative session to discuss how to implement these, possibly before his term ends.

This would be in contrast to the federal government, which has pushed for self-regulation by industry. CAIDP’s Randolph says California could play an important role in setting the floor for AI regulation given that much of the global AI industry is based there.

DAIR’s Hanna says Newsom is not only looking to show a contrast with US President Donald Trump, who believes in self-regulation by firms and last month signed a voluntary accord with several AI leaders, but also with possible Democratic contenders.

“With this, Newsom can look good on the primary debate stage,” she said.

Gallegos, the governor’s spokesperson, told Al Jazeera that “Governor Newsom isn’t interested in virtue-signalling or chasing headlines — he is leading the nation by taking a smarter, strategic, and effective approach to addressing frontier technology”.

Experts say that along with Newsom’s order setting up a committee to examine a kill switch, there is a need for measures for controls across the life cycle to reinforce safety.

“Safety needs to be built in. We issued 12 guidances across the lifecycle when the last ChatGPT model was released. There is a need for safety features throughout the life cycle,” of an AI model, Partnership for AI’s Finlay said.

As Newsom considers such recommendations from California agencies and the expert committee, Ekbia says governments “should take a lesson from what happened with social media. A handful of companies having control were able to do a lot of harm,” and regulate with an anticipatory approach and take on corporate monopolies.

entries.title: Protesters clash with police during nationwide demonstrations in France
entries.summary: Thousands rally in Paris and other cities for demonstrations set to unite students, teachers, unions and 'yellow vests'.
entries.content:
Thousands rally in Paris and other cities for demonstrations set to unite students, teachers, unions and ‘yellow vests’.

Protesters have clashed with police in cities across France as major rallies take place across the country.

Scuffles broke out on Saturday in the capital, Paris, between groups of protesters and police, who used tear gas to push back people wearing hoods and masks.

The demonstrations are set to unite students, teachers, trade unions, and the resurging ‘yellow vest’ movement – remnants of the grassroots cost-of-living protests that shook France in 2018.

Large numbers of riot police were deployed in the Place de la Republique, a square northeast of the city centre, and surrounding streets on Saturday. Dozens of people were reportedly already detained.

Reporting from Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said “a lot” of stun grenades and tear gas were being used by police.

She said that what began as a peaceful protests “never really got started”, as police quickly moved to isolate protesters, effectively trapping them between police lines. “That is where some of the trouble began,” Butler said.

In the southern city of Marseille, meanwhile, local media reported that protesters breached the town hall and looted shops in the city’s commercial district, while in Lyon, media reports said the local tourism office was set ablaze.

This is a “key moment” for France, said Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from the western French city of Rennes.

“There are budget negotiations going on; the French government is trying to find ways to curb its ballooning national debt, and there consequential presidential elections happening next year,” she said.

France’s Interior Ministry had recorded 140 protest actions across the country by midday on Saturday, with 32,800 participants. The ministry said over 250 people had been arrested nationwide so far.

‘Where are we going as a country?’

Saturday’s protests against the rising costs of goods like fuel and food come on the back of weeks of rallies from French high school students, who took to the streets to protest poor conditions in their schools.

Some children who attended those high school protests reported serious injuries at the hands of police, including the case of one 15-year-old girl who lost a hand.

Beyond the clashes at some demonstrations, Saturday has also seen widespread peaceful protests, with unions, teachers, healthcare workers and regular citizens taking to the streets.

French “yellow vest” protesters – who took to the streets in nationwide protests from 2018 to 2020 to protest rising fuels costs – have also signalled that they will join the protests.

The yellow vests have been “trying to make a comeback”, Birchard said, and this “seems to be the moment”.

Bruno Cautres, a researcher at the Paris-based Center for Political Research, told Al Jazeera that Saturday’s events are a “culmination of different mobilisations” including students, teachers, nurses, farmers, yellow vests.

He said the French population is frustrated by high taxes combined with a significant national debt and deficit that prevent the government satisfying their demands: “The French are asking themselves where are we going as a country? How are we going to get out of this budget crisis?”

President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Friday, the eve of the protests.

“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said in Brussels. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”

entries.title: Why Trump’s latest White House press secretary lasted just five days
entries.summary: Katie Zacharia is the shortest-serving White House press secretary after a rocky tenure, but she's not the first to go.
entries.content:
Katie Zacharia is the shortest-serving White House press secretary after a rocky tenure, but she’s not the first to go.

United States President Donald Trump’s latest press secretary has been let go after just five days on the job, following a widely criticised first – and only – White House news conference and amid scrutiny of her credentials.

Trump told reporters on Friday that he believed the press had been harsh towards his new top spokesperson, Katie Zacharia, but that he had advised her to “reconsider” the role.

Shortly after, Al Jazeera and other media confirmed that Zacharia would be “transitioning out” of the position.

That made her the shortest-serving press secretary in US history – even shorter than the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, the former White House communications director who was fired after 10 days on the job during Trump’s first term in office in 2017.

His sacking gave rise to the term “one Scaramucci” – or “a Mooch” – which journalists and White House observers use jokingly as a measure of time to predict how long Trump officials would last in their jobs. Now, a new unit of time – “one Zacharia” – is only half as long.

Recalling his own White House stint this week, Scaramucci wrote on X: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

Here’s what we know about Zacharia’s brief tenure:

Why was Katie Zacharia removed as White House press secretary?

The White House has not given an official reason for Zacharia’s departure, but it came amid mounting concerns about her competency and professional background.

During her first and only news conference on Tuesday, Zacharia appeared uneasy at the podium and struggled at times to get through her sentences. She fumbled her words while looking down at her notes, once confused the words “husband” and “president” and ended the briefing after 14 minutes, taking only three questions from reporters.

Scrutiny intensified after it emerged that Zacharia, who has a law degree and described herself as “an attorney”, had studied law at university but never passed the bar exam required to practice law in the US. She later claimed she had worked as a lawyer in China.

Conservative Fox News host Sean Hannity asked Zacharia during an awkward interview on Thursday: “Why didn’t you just say: ‘I never practised law’?”

Following news of her departure, Zacharia wrote on X that it had been “an honour” to work for Trump, calling him a “kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man”.

How was her one White House briefing received?

Zacharia, who took over from former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, was widely criticised as unpolished and unprepared during her appearance before the White House press corps on Tuesday this week, even by many of Trump’s allies.

During Hannity’s interview with Zacharia, he noted that she had been “widely panned” for her performance.

Conservative journalist and commentator Megyn Kelly said Zacharia needed “to present as a serious person”.

Jen Psaki, a former White House press secretary who worked under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, compared Zacharia’s troubled briefing to a comedy skit. “Maybe this whole White House press secretary thing isn’t really for Katie,” she said. “It’s not for everybody.”

As a fellow White House deportee, Scaramucci gave Zacharia some advice. “Speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor,” he wrote on X.

Who will take over White House press briefings now?

That remains to be seen.

The White House has not announced a permanent replacement, and Trump told Fox News he is “not in a hurry” to fill the role.

The vacancy leaves Trump without a top spokesperson as the US remains mired in a conflict with Iran and heads into crucial midterm elections next month.

How many press secretaries has Trump gone through?

Zacharia was the sixth person to serve as White House press secretary under Trump. He went through four of the officials during his first term and, so far, two in his second.

Zacharia’s predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had held the position since the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025. She resigned in August to spend more time with her children.

Trump’s first-term press secretaries were Kayleigh McEnany, Stephanie Grisham, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Sean Spicer.

McEnany and Spicer now work in media. McEnany hosts several shows on Fox News, while Spicer contributing to NewsNation and has launched his own podcast.

Huckabee Sanders currently serves as the governor of her home state of Arkansas, where she is seeking re-election on November 3.

Grisham left the press secretary position after less than a year in 2020 and became First Lady Melania Trump’s chief of staff. She resigned that role after the January 6, 2021 insurrection and has since become a major critic of the US president.

Which other Trump-appointed officials have been fired?

Zacharia joins a roll call of Trump administration officials to be pushed out during his second term.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece who was previously engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr, was asked to step down from her role earlier this week after reports emerged that she offered a political donor access to senior administration officials in exchange for money.

Earlier in the year, Trump fired Attorney General Pam Bondi amid controversy over her handling of files relating to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which had become a growing political problem for the administration.

A month earlier, Trump ousted Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, after she was grilled in Congress over a $220m advertising campaign and her comments about two US citizens fatally shot by federal officers in Minnesota.

Mike Waltz was one of the first Trump administration officials to be removed during his second term. Waltz was fired as national security adviser in early May 2025 after he mistakenly invited a journalist into a messaging application in which he and other top administration officials discussed military attack plans on Yemen.

entries.title: Child, four women among Palestinians injured in West Bank pogroms
entries.summary: Attacks follow a religious edict by a prominent far-right rabbi permitting the seizure of Palestinian olives.
entries.content:
Attacks across occupied West Bank follow a religious edict by a prominent far-right rabbi permitting the seizure of Palestinian olives.

Several Palestinians have been injured by Israeli settlers, and farmers have been arrested by Israeli forces during Israeli pogroms across the occupied West Bank.

Four women and a child were among six people injured on Saturday when Israeli settlers attacked residents in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS).

In the town of Deir Ammar, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

In the same area, Israeli settlers shot and injured two Palestinians. In the village of Tuqu, southeast of Bethlehem, Israeli forces fired on a Palestinian civilian vehicle.

‘Part of campaign’

In the village of Kafr Malek, northeast of Ramallah, settlers raided a farm at dawn and killed about 20 sheep, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.

He added that Israeli forces had raided the village the previous night as well, firing tear gas canisters that ignited a fire in a house and caused material damage.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah, said settlers destroyed olive trees across the Beit Furik plain, east of Nablus, in the northern West Bank while Israeli forces arrested landowners and olive pickers.

In the village of Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah, she said, settlers under army protection fired live ammunition at farmers in the al-Hariq area to prevent them from completing the harvest and forced them off their land. Settlers also smashed the vehicle of international activist Jonathan Budlak in the village and threw stones at a farmer’s vehicle.

In the village of Burqa near Ramallah, Israeli forces and settlers prevented farmers from picking olives, Odeh said, adding that settlers attacked farmers in the Wadi al-Sha’er area, southeast of Salfit.

“What we see, whether it’s in Beit Furik, Kafr Malek, Deir Jarir or elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, is part of a campaign,” Odeh said.

She said settlers have become increasingly emboldened, publicly advertising attack campaigns on social media platforms.

“There have been 300 documented attacks since the beginning of October, and that has had a devastating impact on a very important season for Palestinian farmers,” she said, adding that danger comes from soldiers and settlers alike as military forces routinely intervene to protect settlers and attack Palestinians defending their land.

Prominent rabbi justifies attacks

The attacks follow a religious edict issued by Rabbi Dov Lior, a prominent rabbi for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and a leading authority among the Hilltop Youth, which is a religious Zionist group devoted to seizing Palestinian land in the West Bank.

In the edict, Lior stated that harvesting olives in the Holy Land is entirely permitted and carries an added virtue, given security dangers.

He wrote that Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish communities to publicly display ownership of the land and fulfil God’s commandment of conquering it. He claimed the land belongs to the Jewish people and Palestinians did not buy or rent it.

Odeh said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu downplays pogroms and no concrete action is taken to stop them.

“It is a matter of debate among politicians, but no one is stopping these settlers, whose names, locations and homes are known,” she said, adding that politicians permit the violence to continue because “it is politically expedient” and secures votes before elections on October 27.

entries.title: Davidovich Fokina stuns top seed Zverev to reach Shanghai Masters final
entries.summary: The 26th-ranked Spaniard fought back to win 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 and will play Daniil Medvedev or Rafael Jodar in the final.
entries.content:
The 26th-ranked Spaniard fought back to win 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 and will play either Daniil Medvedev or Rafael Jodar in the final on Sunday.

Alejandro ‌Davidovich Fokina produced a major upset by defeating top seed Alexander Zverev 5-7 ⁠6-4 6-3 to reach the Shanghai Masters final, where he will face either former world number one Daniil Medvedev or fellow Spaniard Rafael Jodar.

The 25th seed fired ⁠36 winners in the two-hour, two-minute contest on Saturday to secure only his second victory over Zverev in eight meetings. His previous win against the German came in the round of ⁠32 at the Canadian Open in 2023.

Davidovich Fokina earned his first break of the match to take the second set, forcing a decider with a stunning backhand passing shot on the run that capped a bruising baseline exchange and brought the crowd to their feet.

Carrying that momentum into ‌the final set, Davidovich Fokina broke Zverev for a 2-0 lead and never relinquished control, booking a place in the second ATP Masters 1000 final of his career after finishing runner-up in Monte Carlo in 2022.

Landing 82 percent of his first serves and repeatedly exposing Zverev on the forehand side, he secured one of the biggest victories of his career.

“I knew that if I stayed there all match, I could get at least ⁠one chance and I took it there in the second set,” ⁠Davidovich Fokina said.

“Then in the third set, I think I was better physically. The early break in the third set gave me a lot of power.

“I focused on just playing, not mattering about the result but enjoying.”

Zverev said fatigue had caught up with him.

“I think a break is quite necessary now,” the 29-year-old told reporters, saying he would monitor his fitness before a tournament in Vienna that begins October 24.

“I carried a little bit of injury, I carried fatigue into the tournament, and I’m OK to lose to a player like this today,” said Zverev, who had felt his ankle at times in Shanghai.

Davidovich ⁠Fokina, who missed the North American hard-court swing in August because of injury, has now won nine consecutive matches in China after ⁠lifting his second tour-level title at the ATP 250 ⁠event in Chengdu last month.

It was a disappointing end to the week for Zverev, a seven-time ATP Masters 1000 champion whose best result in Shanghai remains his runner-up finish to Medvedev in 2019.

The 29-year-old has otherwise enjoyed a ‌fine season, ending his Grand Slam drought at the French Open before claiming a second major title at the US Open and securing the ATP year-end world number one ranking ‌after ‌Jannik Sinner was sidelined for the remainder of the season with a knee injury.

Fifth-seeded Russian Medvedev was playing 12th-seeded Jodar, 20, in the second semifinal.

entries.title: Hardline Israeli rabbi ruling on stolen Palestinian olives prompts uproar
entries.summary: A controversial ruling by a hardline Israeli rabbi has been condemned by Palestinians.
entries.content:
A hardline religious ruling justifying the theft of Palestinian olive harvests escalates violence and political tensions before Israeli elections.

Prominent Israeli Rabbi Dov Lior issued a Jewish religious ruling on Friday permitting settlers to steal olives from Palestinian orchards in the occupied West Bank.

Lior’s ruling claims that Palestinian landowners who could not access their olives during the harvest season due to Israeli restrictions have been sufficiently compensated in the years they had access to the fruit. According to the ruling, Jews are permitted to pick these olives to claim ownership of the Palestinian land.

Lior, born in Poland in 1933, went as far as classifying the theft of olives from Palestinian farms as an “additional virtue”, as settler pogroms and Israeli occupation continue in the West Bank.

He added that settlers should “conquer the land” far from Jewish communities in order to publicly “demonstrate our ownership” and follow biblical commandment.

“The Jewish people have never given up on the Land of Israel, as we express in our prayers every single day,” the ruling continues. “The Arabs never purchased the land from the Jewish people or from any individual Jew, and therefore it is stolen land in their hands… They never bought it in any way and it remained under the ownership of the Jewish people.”

Harvest violence

The ruling coincides with another wave of settler pogroms against Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest season. On Friday. at least 19 people were injured in 34 attacks by the Israeli military and settlers on Palestinians harvesting their crops across the West Bank.

An American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was assaulted by settlers while covering the daily violence, and five vehicles were torched.

Many Palestinian farmers have been unable to access their crops due to Israeli restrictions and the dangers from the settlers.

While settler pogroms are not exceptional, they come weeks before Israeli elections, with a push by far-right parties to gain the support of settlers and their supporters. But not all Jewish religious leaders backed the call to steal Palestinian olives.

Religious backlash

Rabbis from the religious council of the Gush Etzion settlements published a letter calling the illegal harvesting of Palestinian crops theft, blasphemy, and a moral defect.

Tzohar, an organisation of 800 orthodox rabbis, said in a statement that only the state has the authority to confiscate property. As long as the state recognises Arab ownership of the olives, they belong to them, it added.

Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, told Al Jazeera that there could be political reasons behind the religious groups’ rejection of Rabbi Dov Lior’s comments.

“The position of the other rabbis who rejected this call might be a move driven by political motive and pressure from entities within the government to give the impression that these are anomalous voices that do not represent the general opinion of the settlers.

“The Israeli government is trying to portray that those who carry out these riots are a limited-number group that does not represent public opinion in the settlements, and that the settlers are peaceful, good, and law-abiding, and that the issue is confined to the ‘Hilltop Youth‘ boys who commit these crimes,” he explained.

Rabbi Dov Lior holds immense influence among hardline settler groups, such as the Hilltop Youth, who fiercely back his hardline religious decrees that oppose any territorial compromise with Palestinians.

He is also a prominent figure within Israel’s Religious Zionist movement and serves as the spiritual guide for the far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

“Ben-Gvir relies on the religious rulings of Rabbi Dov Lior, which rely on biblical texts and the Book of Deuteronomy,” Abu Amer noted. He claimed that Rabbi Lior adopts the most extreme interpretations in the Jewish religion.

“There is an important matter, which is that Ben-Gvir competes via the TikTok platform, propaganda, and populist rhetoric, and this is a rhetoric that serves him and brings him votes, given the environment and general atmosphere in Israel after the events of October 7, as there is a ‘market for extremism’ in the Israeli society,” Abu Amer added.

Knesset member Gilad Kariv of the left-wing Democrats Party criticised Lior, accusing him and his followers of dragging Israel into a flood of moral vice.

“Whoever stands on the sidelines in this issue joins the camp of Rabbi Dov Lior and his criminals,” Kariv said.
